{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised by the hxm_program hub's 2026-09-28 field report (art:hxm-program-feedback-2026-09-28), in the owner's own framing: "So far, I've used it mostly as a way to capture tasks at a beamline and a way to troubleshoot issues at a beamline and to document how we solve things. This would be akin to reflow2's /adopt on a set of existing repos, then logging all the issues that arise [in] the actual employment of those projects at the beamline, which usually goes into refining/updating the individual projects. Reflow2 encompasses the full lifecycle of a project, so this use case is included in reflow2, but much more focused on the later phases of deployment and operations and troubleshooting than the initial phases of concept to requirements to design to implementation of design."

WHAT THE SESSION MEASURED: about a fifth of an operations day touched the design graph at all. The rest went to the hub's markdown (task notes, a troubleshooting archive, a host list, a decisions file), because operations knowledge has a home there today. At day's end the hub's own check listed 8 files changed since the export that no reflow2 session reconciled: the design falling behind the operations record. One incident (a motion-controller axis fault) produced zero design nodes.

THE REPORT'S OWN IDEAS for this phase are recorded one per question beside this node: an incident record hung on a named asset (O-17), precedent search over the file archive (O-18), evidence grades such as operator-attested (O-19), an operations mode that ranks incidents and safety first (O-20), and plant-inventory adoption with drift (O-21).

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN:
(a) FIRST-CLASS: operations is the lifecycle's later half and reflow2 serves it. An incident, the evidence gathered, the cause and the fix are design records, and the structure (components, allocations) accretes from what breaks: /adopt running in reverse.
(b) BESIDE THE DESIGN: reflow2 stays the design brain. Incidents live in the tools operations already uses (a tracker, a runbook, the project's files), and the design links to them as artifacts and never holds the log itself.
(c) ONLY WHAT OPERATIONS TEACHES THE DESIGN: the incident log stays outside (files, or a host such as flo2), and reflow2 records what changes the design: the established cause, the failure class, the requirement that was missing, the check that should have caught it. This is the same line drawn today for personas (dec:idea-a-user-carries-a-persona-that-shapes-every-reply): reflow2 keeps the design, a host keeps the rest.
(d) NOTHING NEW: the hub keeps operations in markdown, as today.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, RECORDED BESIDE IT:
· On identity, FOR: the core identity is a person designing without knowing systems engineering. Feeding field reality back into the design is the part of the lifecycle a non-expert knows least, and req:coherence already says the design stays coherent across its lifecycle, not only until it is built.
· On identity, AGAINST: Alex's advice to do fewer things well (dec:idea-reflow2-does-fewer-things-and-does-them-really-well). (a) adds a whole feature family (incidents, inventory, evidence grades, ranking modes) in a space that already has mature tools: issue trackers, maintenance systems, runbooks. That is how a design brain becomes a mediocre maintenance system.
· The measured ratio cuts both ways. A fifth of the work touching the graph can mean reflow2 fails operations, or that most operations work was never design work.
· (c) is the smallest move that keeps the coherence promise, but it depends on someone deciding, mid-incident, which part is design. That is a judgement the report says nobody has time for with the hutch waiting.
· Cost: (a) is large, a new node kind plus its detectors, skills and ranking. (b) is nearly free today, since artifacts already link out.
